## Answer Leak Self-Check

I reviewed the problem text. It contains only the problem statement — no leaked answers, solution sketches, or formalization notes. Proceeding to solve.

## Proof

**Key observation.** For any integer $n > 1$, the divisors of $n$ pair up as $(d, n/d)$, each pair multiplying to $n$. Hence the product of *all* divisors of $n$ equals $n^{d(n)/2}$, where $d(n)$ is the divisor-count function.

The "Sub-Tokens" are all divisors of $n$ except $1$ and $n$ itself. Their product is therefore

$$\frac{n^{d(n)/2}}{1 \cdot n} \;=\; n^{\,d(n)/2 \,-\, 1}.$$

The shipment is **Elite** precisely when this equals $n$:

$$n^{\,d(n)/2 - 1} = n \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \frac{d(n)}{2} - 1 = 1 \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; d(n) = 4.$$

So the Elite ID Numbers are exactly the integers $n>1$ with **exactly four divisors**.

**Characterization of numbers with four divisors.** If $n = p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$, then $d(n) = (a_1+1)\cdots(a_r+1) = 4$. The only factorizations of $4$ are $4$ and $2\cdot 2$, giving:
- $n = p^3$ (a prime cube), or
- $n = p\,q$ (a product of two distinct primes).

**Enumerating the first ten, in increasing order.** Checking each integer from $2$ upward, keeping only those of the forms $p^3$ or $p\,q$:

| # | $n$ | form | divisors |
|---|-----|------|----------|
| 1 | 6  | $2\cdot 3$  | 1,2,3,6 |
| 2 | 8  | $2^3$       | 1,2,4,8 |
| 3 | 10 | $2\cdot 5$  | 1,2,5,10 |
| 4 | 14 | $2\cdot 7$  | 1,2,7,14 |
| 5 | 15 | $3\cdot 5$  | 1,3,5,15 |
| 6 | 21 | $3\cdot 7$  | 1,3,7,21 |
| 7 | 22 | $2\cdot 11$ | 1,2,11,22 |
| 8 | 26 | $2\cdot 13$ | 1,2,13,26 |
| 9 | 27 | $3^3$       | 1,3,9,27 |
| 10| 33 | $3\cdot 11$ | 1,3,11,33 |

All skipped integers ($2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,16,17,18,19,20,23,24,25,28,29,30,31,32$) have divisor counts $\ne 4$: primes have $2$, prime-squares $p^2$ have $3$, and composites with $\ge 3$ prime factors or exponents $\ge 4$ have $\ge 5$ (verified case by case above).

**Sum:**

$$6+8+10+14+15+21+22+26+27+33 = 182.$$

The sum of the ID Numbers of the first ten Elite shipments is $\boxed{182}$.
